xml-to-csv.assumptionNote: Assumes your XML has repeating sibling elements (records) with flat child elements (columns). Nested elements and attributes are skipped.
benefits: Move XML data — feeds, exports, configs — into spreadsheets in seconds.
No need to write a one-off Python or XSLT script for a simple conversion.
Automatic record detection handles most real-world XML without configuration.
Files under 5 MB parse instantly, entirely on your device.

faqs.a: It looks for the most common repeating element. If your XML is <catalog> with many <book> children, each <book> becomes a row. For deeper structures it picks the tag name that repeats most.
faqs.q: How does it find my records?

faqs.a: They are ignored — only element text becomes CSV cells. If your data lives in attributes (like <book title="...">), restructure it to child elements first.
Only direct leaf child elements become columns. Nested elements (a child that itself contains elements) are skipped, and so are attributes. Flatten your XML one level if you need that data.
Yes — use the upload button for any .xml file up to 5 MB. The content is read locally and never sent anywhere.
faqs.q: Can I upload an XML file instead of pasting?

faqs.a: Yes. The CSV uses standard quoting and UTF-8 encoding with a BOM so Excel detects it automatically. If characters still look wrong, open it in Excel via Data > From Text/CSV and pick UTF-8.
faqs.q: Will Excel open the CSV correctly?

faqs.a: No. Parsing is done by your browser's built-in XML parser. Your data never leaves your device.

xml-to-csv.formula:
records = all elements with the most common repeating tag (e.g. <book>).
columns = union of leaf child tag names across records, in first-seen order.
cell(record, column) = text of the matching child, trimmed.
CSV cell escaping: if the value contains a comma, quote, or newline -> wrap in "..." and double inner quotes.
howTo: Paste your XML into the text box, upload an .xml file, or load the sample.
The tool parses the XML and shows how many records and columns it found, plus the record element name.
Preview the first rows, toggle the header row on or off if you need to.
Copy the CSV or download it as a .csv file and open it in Excel or Google Sheets.
keyFacts: Records are detected automatically: the tool finds the repeating element (like <book> or <item>) and treats each occurrence as one row.
Columns come from the child elements of each record — <title>, <author>, <price> become the CSV headers.
CSV follows the standard: commas, quotes, and newlines inside values are escaped with double quotes.
Namespaces are stripped from tag names, so <ns:title> becomes the column 'title'.
Only leaf elements become columns; nested structures are skipped to keep the table flat.

limitations: Deeply nested XML is flattened poorly — only one level of child elements becomes columns; deeper nesting is skipped.
XML attributes are ignored; only element text becomes CSV data.
Huge XML files (over 5 MB) are not accepted to keep the browser responsive.
Invalid XML (unclosed tags, stray & characters) will not parse — fix it with an XML validator first.

xml-to-csv.quickAnswer: Paste your XML (or upload an .xml file) and the tool finds the repeating elements — for example the <book> entries inside <catalog> — treats each one as a row, and turns their child elements (<title>, <author>, <price>) into CSV columns. Two books become a header row plus two data rows you can open in Excel or Google Sheets.
xml-to-csv.tagline: Turn XML data into a clean CSV table — paste XML or upload a file, download the spreadsheet-ready result.
xml-to-csv.workedExample:
XML:
<catalog>
  <book><title>Atomic Habits</title><author>James Clear</author><price>499</price></book>
  <book><title>Deep Work</title><author>Cal Newport</author><price>450</price></book>
</catalog>

1. Repeating element: <book> appears twice -> 2 records.
2. Leaf children: title, author, price -> 3 columns.
3. CSV output:
title,author,price
Atomic Habits,James Clear,499
Deep Work,Cal Newport,450
